overview:
Russia is by far the largest country on Earth, covering about an eighth of the world's land and stretching across eleven time zones from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean. It is nearly twice the size of the United States and shares borders with fourteen countries. The Ural Mountains divide it into European Russia in the west, where most people live, and Siberia in the east.

About 145 million people live in Russia and speak Russian, written in the Cyrillic alphabet, while more than a hundred other languages are spoken by peoples across the country. Moscow, the capital, has the Kremlin fortress and Red Square at its heart and a subway system whose older stations look like marble palaces. Saint Petersburg, built on marshy islands, is a city of canals and imperial palaces.

Russia is a federal republic with a powerful presidency, and it is a leading producer of oil, natural gas, wheat, and metals.
landAndNature: Siberia is a world of its own: taiga, the largest forest on the planet, runs for thousands of kilometers in larch and pine before giving way to treeless tundra, frozen underground as permafrost. Winters in Yakutia fall below minus 50 degrees Celsius, among the coldest anywhere people live. Lake Baikal, a crack in the Earth's crust filled 1,642 meters deep, holds roughly a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh water and its own species of freshwater seal. The Volga, Europe's longest river, waters the west, while the Kamchatka Peninsula in the far east bristles with active volcanoes and geysers. Siberian tigers, brown bears, reindeer, and sables live in the forests.
peopleAndCulture: Russia is home to many peoples besides Russians, among them Tatars, Chechens, Bashkirs, Buryats, and reindeer-herding Nenets in the Arctic. Orthodox Christianity and Islam are the largest faiths. Meals often open with soup, whether beet borscht or fish solyanka, followed by pelmeni dumplings, blini pancakes, and dark rye bread. Russian writers such as Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, and Chekhov are read everywhere, and the Bolshoi and Mariinsky theaters made Russian ballet world-famous. Chess is taught in schools, while ice hockey and figure skating draw huge audiences. New Year, with a decorated tree and Grandfather Frost, is the biggest holiday, and the banya, a hot steam bath, is a weekly ritual.
history: Slavic peoples settled the plains, and the state of Kievan Rus took shape around Kyiv in the 800s, adopting Orthodox Christianity in 988. Mongol armies overran it in the 1200s. Moscow later grew into the center of power, and in 1547 Ivan IV was crowned tsar; Peter the Great and Catherine the Great pushed the empire across Siberia to the Pacific. Revolution in 1917 overthrew the last tsar and brought the communists to power, creating the Soviet Union. Under Stalin, industry grew quickly while millions died in famines and political purges. The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people defeating Nazi Germany in World War II, then rivaled the United States through the Cold War. It broke into fifteen countries in 1991. Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and the war has continued since.
funFacts: The Trans-Siberian Railway runs about 9,300 kilometers from Moscow to Vladivostok, a trip of roughly seven days.
Lake Baikal holds around a fifth of all the liquid fresh water on Earth and freezes clear enough to see down into it.
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite, in 1957, and Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space in 1961.
Russia is so wide that when the day begins in Kamchatka, clocks in Moscow are still nine hours behind.
Matryoshka nesting dolls, now a symbol of Russia, were first carved only in the 1890s.
